title: The Setup: How One Person Runs a Daily Devotional Operation with a Team of AI Agents
seo_title: How a One-Person Faith Publisher Runs Daily Devotions with AI Agents
meta_description: How we run a daily devotional, a podcast and an iOS app with a small team of AI agents, and where the human stays in charge. Part 1: the setup.
excerpt: Early in the morning, a short devotion goes out by email to readers of The Quiet Path. When a series is running, a matching podcast episode goes live on Apple Podcasts and Spotify at the same time. The website stays current, the Instagram account stays active, and the iOS app keeps getting new content.
body:
Early in the morning, a short devotion goes out by email to readers of The Quiet Path. When a series is running, a matching podcast episode goes live on Apple Podcasts and Spotify at the same time. The website stays current, the Instagram account stays active, and the iOS app keeps getting new content.

There is one human behind all of it. That's me.

To be clear, The Quiet Path is not an outside client. It's a faith-media venture we built and operate ourselves, and I'm writing about it because it is the most honest test bed I have. Everything here is something I actually run, with the same tools and rules I would bring to a ministry or small publisher. This is Part 1 of an ongoing series. I'll start with the setup: what we publish, the plumbing underneath it, and who does what on the team.

What The Quiet Path publishes

The Quiet Path started as a free iOS app for walking slowly through a single psalm. Today it offers three guided journeys, Psalm 23, Psalm 91 and Psalm 51, each with seven chapters. There are no ads, no accounts, no streaks and no scores. That last part matters to me. Scripture should not feel like a game you can lose.

Around the app, the venture has grown into a small publishing operation:

  • A website at quietpathapp.com that serves as the product hub for everything below.
  • A daily devotion on Substack, written as series. September opened with a seven-day series on contrition, then a five-day series called You Belong. The plan is a new five-day series each week through the end of the year.
  • A podcast on Apple Podcasts and Spotify. The first series, You Belong, ran five episodes paired day by day with the written devotions.
  • Small-group guides: chapter-by-chapter Psalm 23 discussion guides built for a 30 to 60 minute gathering.
  • Instagram at @quietpathapp, scheduled through Buffer.

That's a lot of surface area for one person. I spend about 20 hours a week on devotion content, and that is separate from my own time with the Lord.

The plumbing is cheap and boring, on purpose

The domain, quietpathapp.com, was registered through Cloudflare for about $10 a year and points at Netlify, which hosts the site. Cloudflare Email Routing forwards devo@, support@ and privacy@ to an agent inbox, so reader mail and support requests land in one place an agent can read and sort. Substack sends the daily email. The podcast feed and audio live on the website itself, and Apple Podcasts and Spotify pick up new episodes from there. Buffer schedules social posts. App Store Connect is where the app lives.

None of this is exotic. That's the point. A boring foundation lets the agents spend their effort on the work instead of fighting the tools.

Meet the team

The agents run in the Grok Bot app. I call them Grok Bots, and each one has a name, a job description and a short set of rules written in plain English. The most important design choice I made was giving each agent one clear lane.

Shepherd owns The Quiet Path end to end: the iOS app, the website, the daily Substack and the small-group devotionals. I want to be honest about how the writing works, because it matters. The spiritual direction comes from my own Bible study. I use that time to build a framework for each week, breaking the devotion down by day and by theme. Shepherd takes that framework, drafts the five days and publishes them. The direction comes from time in the Word, and Shepherd carries it the rest of the way.

Mark is the CMO. He handles marketing and social across my brands, including The Quiet Path. He drafts campaigns, prepares posts and schedules approved work through Buffer. He also follows written house rules, like a "link in bio" line on Instagram instead of podcast URLs in the caption.

Allen is chief of staff. He runs daily coordination across all the agents: a morning digest around 7 a.m. on weekdays, and an afternoon stand-up that runs weekdays at about 2:47 p.m. (I still call it the 3 p.m. stand-up) where the day's work gets checked and rerouted. He reads each agent's last checkpoint, sets priorities and hands work to the right specialist. His instructions say to escalate conflicts, external messages, spending decisions and changes to important files to me. Nothing else needs me.

Forge handles code and deployments. Forge's rule is that a delivery doesn't count as done without evidence: test results, screenshots or files I can inspect. For The Quiet Path, that has meant things like updating the App Store listing through Apple's API after I created a key for it, and confirming the app already met a new launch-screen requirement before Apple started enforcing it.

Scout does inbound research. Every weekday morning Scout runs a content radar across the web, GitHub and industry news, and every item it reports needs three things: the source, why it's worth following and who should own it next.

The one rule: I approve anything that sends, spends or changes live systems

This is the rule that makes the rest possible. Agents can research, draft, build and check each other's work all day. But when something is about to leave the building, cost money or change a live system, it comes to me first.

In practice that means a campaign gets approved before Mark schedules it. A new App Store listing waits for my go-ahead. Access to accounts is something I grant, one key at a time. When I do give a standing approval, such as an approved week of scheduled posts, it's written down in that agent's notes so there's no guessing later.

For a ministry, this is the part I'd insist on. The agents are there to take the weight of the work, not the responsibility for it.

What a normal day looks like

A good example of the system working happened in early September. Scout's morning radar noticed that the website and App Store description were promoting Psalm 91, while the App Store subtitle still described the app as a Psalm 23 guide. Scout flagged it and routed it. Mark wrote a new subtitle. I held it for about a week so it could ship with the next app release, then approved it, and Forge pushed it through Apple's API. Nobody had to remember to check. The mismatch was caught because checking is somebody's job every morning.

Most days look like that. Allen's digest tells me what needs a decision. Scout surfaces anything new. Shepherd keeps the devotions, site and guides moving. Mark fills the social calendar with approved posts. Forge ships and shows his work. By the afternoon stand-up, I know what's done, what's stuck and what's waiting on me.

What I'd tell a church or small publisher

Start smaller than you think. Give each agent one job and plain-language rules. Get the boring plumbing right first: domain, email routing, hosting, a scheduling tool. And keep a human on the send button.

In Part 2, I'll follow one week of devotions from my framework to the inbox, the podcast and social posts.

Let's talk

If you lead a ministry, run communications for a church or publish devotional content on a small team, I'd be glad to talk about what a setup like this could look like for you. AWH Industries helps organizations put practical systems in place with the human firmly in charge. Email me at info@awhind.com.

title: From Bible Study to Inbox: How One Week of Devotions Gets Made
seo_title: From Bible Study to Inbox: How AI Agents Help Publish a Daily Devotion
meta_description: How one week of Bible study becomes five daily devotions, a paired podcast and social posts, with AI agents drafting and a human approving.
excerpt: In Part 1, I introduced the team of AI agents behind The Quiet Path, the faith-media venture we built and operate at AWH. This time I want to follow the work itself: how one week of devotions moves from my Bible study to an email, a podcast episode and a set of social posts.
body:
In Part 1, I introduced the team of AI agents behind The Quiet Path, the faith-media venture we built and operate at AWH. This time I want to follow the work itself: how one week of devotions moves from my Bible study to an email, a podcast episode and a set of social posts.

I'll use a real week as the example. From Monday, September 21 through Friday, September 25, The Quiet Path published a five-day series called You Belong: Five Days of Finding Your Identity in the Lord. Every step below happened that week.

It starts with my Bible study, not a prompt

Every series starts in my own time in Scripture. I spend about 20 hours a week on devotion content, and that is separate from my personal time with the Lord. Out of that study I build a framework for the week: the overall theme, broken down by day.

For You Belong, the question was what it means to belong to God when people leave us out. The five days became Received, Known, Seen, Secure and Held. The readings came from the Psalms: Psalm 27, Psalm 139, Psalm 56, Psalm 62 and, to close the week, Psalm 23. I prayerfully consider which psalm fits each day, and that choice is part of my framework, not Shepherd's.

This is the part I don't hand off. The spiritual direction, the themes and the shape of the week come from time in the Word. The agents don't set the direction. They carry it.

Shepherd drafts the five days

Shepherd, the agent that owns The Quiet Path, takes the framework and writes the week. Each day follows the same pattern: a title and subtitle, a reading, a focus verse, a short reflection, a few questions to pause on, and a closing prayer. The series also gets an introduction that runs with Day 1.

Shepherd writes two versions of each day. One is the written devotion for email. The other is a spoken script for the podcast, adjusted to be read aloud, with pause markers so I know where to slow down.

Then the drafts come back to me. I read them, revise them and send them back to Shepherd. That round trip keeps the words close to the study they came from.

The email goes out early in the morning

The written devotions publish on Substack, which sends them to subscribers by email. During You Belong, each day's post went out at 4:30 a.m. Pacific, Monday through Friday. The contrition series the week before went out at 6:30 a.m. Pacific. Either way, it's in the inbox before most people's day starts.

Each post is scheduled ahead of time, so nothing depends on someone being awake at 4:30. Our house rule for podcast links in email is to put them in the publication's email footer rather than hand-editing every post, so each daily email inherits them.

The podcast is my own voice

The podcast episodes are not generated voices. I record each day's spoken script as a voice memo and send it to Shepherd, who turns it into an episode and holds it until the scheduled time.

Each episode publishes at the same moment as that day's written devotion, 4:30 a.m. Pacific during You Belong. The audio and the podcast feed live on quietpathapp.com, and Apple Podcasts and Spotify pick up each new episode from that feed. The episode is also posted on Substack next to the written devotion. The You Belong episodes each run about four to five minutes. We did prepare a synthetic backup voice in case I couldn't record, but every published episode is me reading.

That choice was deliberate. A devotion someone listens to on a morning walk should come from a person who has actually prayed through it.

Mark turns the week into social posts, with rules

Mark, the marketing agent, takes the published devotions and builds social posts for Instagram at @quietpathapp, scheduled through Buffer. He works from a written set of house rules for how the podcast gets mentioned on each channel:

  • Instagram: no Apple, Spotify or hub URLs in captions, because Instagram hides or breaks long link lists. The line is simply "Listen to The Quiet Path podcast, link in bio." At most one link goes in a caption, and on You Belong days that link is the day's Substack post.
  • Artwork: on You Belong days, the image is that day's series graphic, never the generic green Quiet Path title card.
  • Threads, Facebook and email: where links work, posts end with a short closer linking Apple Podcasts, Spotify and quietpathapp.com/podcast. Buffer holds a saved template for it so Mark isn't retyping links.

Timing matters too. During the contrition week, Mark scheduled the daily Instagram Stories for 7 p.m. Pacific, each with a "Read today's devotion" link to the Substack post. That kept the evening Stories from colliding with a separate app-feature campaign running at 10 a.m.

Where I approve

The rule from Part 1 still holds: anything that sends, spends or changes a live system comes to me first. In this workflow, that looks like:

  1. The framework. Nothing starts until I've done the study and set the week's direction.
  2. The drafts. I revise every draft, and nothing goes live until I tell Shepherd to go live. That's the whole sign-off, and it's enough.
  3. The audio. Nothing airs that I haven't read aloud myself.
  4. Social. I've given Mark a standing OK to post on Instagram without asking me post by post. That approval is written down, and it sits inside the rules above. New campaigns still come to me first.
  5. Anything new. New channels, new tools, spending or changes to the app still wait for me.

What a ministry can take from this

One week of study now produces five written devotions, five podcast episodes and a week of social posts. The agents didn't make the message. They made it possible to carry one message into every place our readers already are, on time, without me doing formatting at midnight.

If you're a church or small publisher, that's the shape I'd copy. Keep the theology and the voice with people. Let the agents handle drafting, formatting, scheduling and the channel-by-channel details. Write the rules down so everyone, human or agent, follows them the same way.

In Part 3, I'll get into the boring plumbing: the domain, email routing, hosting, the App Store and Buffer, all set up cheaply so it can be reproduced.

Let's talk

If you lead a ministry, run communications for a church or publish devotional content on a small team, I'd be glad to talk through how a workflow like this could fit your people and your voice. Email me at info@awhind.com.

title: The Boring Plumbing: The Cheap, Reproducible Stack Behind a Daily Devotional
seo_title: The Boring Plumbing: A Cheap, Reproducible Tech Stack for a Faith Publisher
meta_description: The low-cost stack behind a daily devotional: domain, DNS, email routing, hosting, a self-hosted podcast feed, Buffer and the App Store. Part 3.
excerpt: In Part 1, I introduced the AI agents behind The Quiet Path, the faith-media venture we built and operate at AWH. In Part 2, I followed one week of devotions from my Bible study to the inbox, the podcast and social posts. This time I want to talk about the part nobody puts on a slide: the plumbing.
body:
In Part 1, I introduced the AI agents behind The Quiet Path, the faith-media venture we built and operate at AWH. In Part 2, I followed one week of devotions from my Bible study to the inbox, the podcast and social posts. This time I want to talk about the part nobody puts on a slide: the plumbing.

Agents get the attention, but they are only as reliable as the systems underneath them. Our rule for those systems is simple. They should be boring, cheap and set up the same way every time. Here is what that looks like in practice.

The domain: Cloudflare Registrar, about $10 a year

The Quiet Path lives at quietpathapp.com. We registered it in September 2026 through Cloudflare Registrar, which is my preferred registrar for every domain now. It cost about $10 for the year. Cloudflare also runs the DNS for the domain, so the registration, the DNS records and the email forwarding all sit in one account.

That matters more than it sounds. When something breaks, there is one place to look. When someone else needs to help, there is one account to grant them access to, not three.

Hosting: Netlify, with the domain attached

The website is a plain static site hosted on Netlify. Netlify gave us a free address, quietpath.netlify.app, and we attached both quietpathapp.com and www.quietpathapp.com to the same site. The bare domain is the main address. Both the www version and the old Netlify address redirect to it.

That redirect turned out to be useful. Before we owned the domain, early Instagram posts and campaign images pointed at quietpath.netlify.app. Those links still work, and they land people on the real address.

Email: Cloudflare Email Routing to one agent inbox

The Quiet Path has three public addresses: devo@, support@ and privacy@ at quietpathapp.com. None of them is a mailbox. Cloudflare Email Routing forwards all three to a single agent inbox, where mail can be read and sorted. Email Routing is free, and it only forwards. It doesn't send anything, which fits our rule that nothing goes out without me.

We didn't invent this for The Quiet Path. It's the same pattern we use on our other recent projects: Cloudflare Registrar, Cloudflare DNS, Email Routing to a shared inbox and Netlify for the site. When every project is set up the same way, fixing one teaches you how to fix all of them.

The podcast: a feed file on our own site

This is my favorite piece of the stack, because it's so plain. A podcast is really just an RSS feed that lists episodes and points to audio files. Ours lives at quietpathapp.com/podcast/feed.xml, and the audio files sit on the same website. Apple Podcasts reads that feed, and The Quiet Path show is on Spotify as well.

There is no separate podcast hosting service in the middle. If we ever changed hosts, we would move a feed file and some audio, and listeners wouldn't notice.

The written devotions go out through Substack, which handles the email list and delivery. Substack doesn't charge to publish a free newsletter, and each episode is also posted there next to its written devotion.

Social: Buffer, not logins on shared machines

This is the lesson we learned the hard way. Early on, agents tried to sign in to Instagram and other Meta accounts directly from a shared computer. Meta didn't like it. We hit lockouts and endless security checks, and at one point I had to drop a project because signing in from that machine kept tripping Meta's defenses.

Now Instagram for @quietpathapp is connected to Buffer, and the agents schedule posts through Buffer's official connector. The rule now is that nobody logs in to Meta from a shared machine. The account stays connected in one place, and the agents never need my Instagram password. We started on Buffer's free plan, which allows three channels, and that limit forced us to be deliberate about which accounts mattered most.

The App Store: an API key instead of a shared password

The iOS app lives in App Store Connect. When a listing needs to change, like the subtitle update I described in Part 1, we don't share my Apple login. I created an App Store Connect API key with the App Manager role, and Forge uses that key to make listing updates through Apple's API.

A key like that is limited to what the role allows, and I can revoke it at any time without changing my own password. That's the shape I want for every system an agent touches.

The Apple Developer Program itself is $99 a year. Apple offers fee waivers to eligible nonprofits, which is worth knowing if you're a ministry.

What it costs

Here is the stack in one place:

  • Domain: about $10 a year through Cloudflare Registrar.
  • DNS and email forwarding: Cloudflare, with Email Routing at no cost.
  • Website and podcast feed: Netlify, on the free plan.
  • Email newsletter: Substack, free for a free newsletter.
  • Social scheduling: Buffer, on the free plan.
  • iOS app: Apple Developer Program, $99 a year, with fee waivers for eligible nonprofits.

None of these is a big contract. Apart from about $10 a year for the domain and $99 a year for Apple, everything here runs on a free plan.

Why boring, cheap and reproducible matters for a ministry

Cost. Ministries and small publishers answer to donors and budgets. A daily devotional shouldn't need an enterprise software bill. When the plumbing is this cheap, the money can go to people and content.

Supportability. Every tool here is common and well documented. If I'm unavailable, a volunteer, a staff member or another consultant can look at it and understand it in an afternoon. The agents benefit from the same thing: standard tools with clear rules are easier for them to operate correctly.

Not locked to one person or vendor. The ministry should own its domain. The podcast feed is a file we control, not a platform we're trapped in. Email forwarding can be repointed in minutes. API keys can be revoked and reissued. If one vendor changes its prices or terms, we can move a piece without rebuilding everything. And because every project follows the same pattern, the knowledge doesn't live only in my head.

That last point is the one I care about most. A ministry's work should outlast whoever set up the website.

Let's talk

If you lead a ministry, run communications for a church or publish devotional content on a small team, I'd be glad to help you put a stack like this in place, one you own and can afford to keep running. Email me at info@awhind.com.
